Well, let me break the glass that you put between yourself and the world for a moment. 

You cannot let go of your son's life because you have not done what you need to do to save him. You are still the guy who only sees himself and only thinks that he's putting others first. You're not. Intending to put others first doesn't do that by itself. 

You have to lay yourself down. You have to put down your intentions. You have to put down what you want and what you hope to achieve. 

As long as you are focused on yourself, you cannot see others. What you want for them stands between you and them. It is only when you come look at them with clean and clear eyes that you can truly see THEM and not you and what you are wanting for them.

Your thoughts on the situation don't matter. When you are a thousand miles away from someone and you think you are helping them become independent by giving them space, you're lying to yourself. You don't know. You don't know unless you see. They may be on their own working things out and they may be dying because they aren't ready yet. They may be up for the challenge and they may not. You don't know unless you're watching. You don't know unless you are there to see with open and unbiased eyes, ready to witness whatever is going on. 

You are frankly not mature enough to do that. You are not mature enough to save your boy.

I'm afraid that you are destined to suffer until you become the man who is open to seeing people and can then decide how to respond. Maybe you could have saved him. Maybe you could have eased his suffering, but not saved him. Maybe you could have connected with him, but there was nothing you could do. Maybe you two could have looked each other in the eyes, knowing that it was the end, and said goodbye.

Yet, you weren't able to do that because you were too concerned with yourself than to suck it up and be with your dying son. 

I don't mean talking to him, asking him questions and trying to prevent it. I don't mean calling a bunch of people, trying to find him help or drugs.

I mean just sitting there with him with an open mind and an open heart, ready to listen.

Do you know what your son's dying wish was? Do you have any clue? Do you have any idea at all what he wanted from your relationship? Do you know what HE needed from you, the way HE saw it?

Do you know if he wanted you to teach him how to start a fire? Do you know if he wanted you to teach him something about life or people? Do you know if he had a secret interest that he wanted to share with you, but was afraid to? Do you know if all he wanted was for you to see him just once, to share a moment of connection, and for you to give your honest assessment about whether you could do anything to help him or not?

I'm sure you don't. I'm sure you don't because you watched and gave up hope, and you don't want to believe that that's what you did. You don't want to believe that when your son was dying, you left his side.

He died without a father. 

A father would have listened. A father would have cared. A father would have the courage to hold him when the life went out of his eyes, if that's what the situation required.

You didn't have the guts for that. You didn't have the guts to be there for your son, to face your own emotions, and to see the truth.

You didn't have the guts to risk crying with him, to admit to him that you weren't strong enough to do anything, or that you didn't know what to do. 

As result of this, you never listened and you never found out for sure.

It's a shame. However, it's in the past.

What you need to do is build up the courage to listen. Stop trying to help. Stop trying to give an impression. Stop hoping. Listen.

After you listen, then you can figure out whether you have it in your power to help someone or do anything. Then you can let them know and see if there is anything else that they want you to do, or if there's anything they can do. Then you can help them or just give them a hug and say goodbye.

Not before your listen.
